newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss activist claims court win over Scientology.
newsitem.headline: Swiss activist claims court win over Scientology.

text.p: A Swiss anti-sect campaigner claimed victory in her fight against the Church of Scientology on Thursday after a cantonal court said an insulted Scientologist could not use anti-racism laws to punish her outspoken views.

A Scientology lawyer blasted the verdict as "absolutely political" and the plaintiff -- an architect who took umbrage at the activist's railing against the sect at a local school -- said he was considering an appeal to the highest Swiss court.

"I am not jumping for joy because I think of the very many people affected, the parents, marriage partners and children involved," said activist Elsbeth Bates, of Altstaetten in the eastern canton of St Gallen.

"I am very much aware of how much pain and sorrow this has cost them. That is why I am not jumping up and down for joy, but I am certainly very happy. It was a decision from this court that took lots of courage."
In a verdict published this week, the court ruled Scientology could not be considered a religion under the anti-racism law and so the plaintiff, Donat Roth, could not use it to silence Bates.

"The application of this penal law against racial discrimination would be stretched too far if adherents of ideological groups that describe themselves as subscribing to a religious philosophy -- or even better: ideology -- can invoke it," the court ruled.
"In describing itself, the reverent relation of people to God is lacking," the court found, adding it was also not generally recognised as a religion by the Swiss population.
"In my view this is an absolutely political verdict," countered Gabriela Arm, a lawyer for Scientology in Zurich.

"This verdict ignores European verdicts on Scientology. There are two well known verdicts of the European Human Rights Comission that say very clearly that Scientology is a religious coummunity, and this simply ignores that."

She said local officials in St Gallen were trying to use the verdict to force the Federal Court, Switzerland's highest tribunal, to issue a ruling on Scientology, which she said had 5,000 members in Switzerland.
Arm said the cantonal court had improperly disregarded testimony supporting Scientology's stance.

"Church of Scientology articles of faith speak very clearly of God," she said. "Testimony from religious experts that was submitted was simply ignored and says clearly that Scientology is a religion by definition because it believes in a higher being and deals with the spiritual side of people."

The case began after Bates, co-founder of an organisation called Swiss Working Group Against Destructive Cults, criticised Scientology in front of a secondary school class and handed out stickers bearing skulls and words criticising the organisation.
"A group like Scientology and very many others is hiding behind the front of religion," she told Reuters.
"The whole thing is not about religion. It is not about religious ideology or a God or whatever you want to call it. The thing behind it is to make money and more money. Scientology is a business."
Scientology, which counts Hollywood stars and other celebrities among its members, has been fighting running battle in Europe for recognition as a religion, as it has won in the United States.
It was founded in 1954 by the American science fiction writer L. Ron Hubbard, who said he had discovered the science of mental health.
